title: O-Level Combined Science Physics: Half-Life and Background Radiation
topic: Nature of Background Radiation, Corrected Count Rates, and Half-Life Calculations
subject: Combined Physics

questions.question: Which of the following statements best defines background radiation?
options: Radiation present in the environment all the time
Radiation only found inside nuclear reactors
Radiation produced exclusively by medical equipment
Cosmic rays that only strike Earth during solar flares
questions.explanation: Background radiation is the low-level ionizing radiation that is continuously present in the surrounding environment from both natural and artificial sources.

questions.question: Which of the following is a major natural source of background radiation found trapped in rocks and soil?
questions.explanation: Radon gas is a naturally occurring radioactive gas produced by the decay of trace amounts of uranium found embedded within rocks and soil.

questions.question: Which of the following is classified as an artificial or man-made source of background radiation?
options: Radioactive gases from granite building blocks
Potassium isotopes found naturally inside food crops
questions.explanation: Medical procedures, such as diagnostic X-rays and radiation therapies, represent artificial sources of background radiation introduced into the environment by human technology.

questions.question: A student measures the radiation in a room when no experimental radioactive sources are present. What is the detector recording?
questions.explanation: Even in the complete absence of a test source, a radiation detector will always record a non-zero value due to ambient background radiation existing in the room.

questions.question: Why must background radiation be measured and subtracted during a laboratory radioactivity experiment?
options: To find the true count rate of the source
To increase the half-life of the sample
To prevent the sensor tube from overheating
To change alpha emissions into safe gamma rays
questions.explanation: Subtracting the background count rate from the total measured count rate yields the corrected count rate, which isolates the true radiation output of the source.

questions.question: Which device is commonly connected to a digital counter to measure background radiation count rates?
questions.explanation: A Geiger-Muller (GM) tube is the standard laboratory instrument used to detect ionizing radiation particles and pulses, which are then logged by a counter.

questions.question: What unit is typically used to describe the frequency of radiation pulses detected over a specific interval?
questions.explanation: Radiation count rates are expressed as the number of ionization events or pulses recorded per unit time, most commonly as counts per minute or counts per second.

questions.question: The background count rate is 30 counts per minute. A detector reads a total of 150 counts per minute near a radioactive source. Find the corrected count rate.
questions.explanation: Corrected count rate equals total measured count rate minus the background count rate. Calculation: 150 minus 30 equals 120 counts per minute.

questions.question: Which statement best defines the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
options: The time taken for half the unstable nuclei to decay
Half the total lifespan of a chemical element sample
The time required for an isotope to double its protons
The total seconds a particle takes to move one meter
questions.explanation: Half-life is strictly defined as the time taken for half the unstable radioactive nuclei present in a sample to undergo decay.

questions.question: After exactly one half-life has passed, what fraction of the original unstable radioactive nuclei remains undecayed?
questions.explanation: By definition, one half-life represents the time duration required for the number of radioactive nuclei to be halved, leaving exactly one-half of the starting sample undecayed.

questions.question: A sample of a radioactive isotope contains 800 unstable nuclei. How many unstable nuclei will remain after exactly two half-lives have elapsed?
questions.explanation: After the first half-life, the count drops from 800 to 400. After the second half-life, the remaining 400 is halved again, which leaves 200 unstable nuclei.

questions.question: What fraction of a radioactive isotope sample remains undecayed after a total of three half-lives have passed?
questions.explanation: The fraction remaining decreases exponentially: after 1 half-life it is one-half, after 2 half-lives it is one-quarter, and after 3 half-lives it is one-eighth.

questions.question: A source has an initial corrected count rate of 400 counts per minute. If its half-life is 10 minutes, what will its corrected count rate be after 30 minutes?
questions.explanation: A time span of 30 minutes represents exactly 3 half-lives (30 divided by 10). Halving the activity three times sequentially: 400 to 200, then to 100, and finally to 50 counts per minute.

questions.question: A pure sample of a radioactive isotope has an initial mass of 24 g. If it undergoes decay for four half-lives, what mass of the isotope remains unreacted?
questions.explanation: After four half-lives, the remaining mass is one-sixteenth of the starting mass. Calculation: 24 g divided by 16 equals 1.5 g.

questions.question: An isotope sample has decayed until only one-sixteenth of its original activity remains. How many half-lives have passed during this period?
questions.explanation: Since one-half multiplied by one-half multiplied by one-half multiplied by one-half equals one-sixteenth, a reduction to one-sixteenth means exactly four half-lives have occurred.

questions.question: The corrected count rate of a sample drops from 800 counts per second to 100 counts per second over a span of 12 hours. Calculate the half-life.
questions.explanation: Dropping from 800 to 100 requires a division factor of 8, which corresponds to 3 half-lives (2 multiplied by 2 multiplied by 2). If 3 half-lives equal 12 hours, then 1 half-life equals 12 divided by 3, which is 4 hours.

questions.question: A radioactive tracer has a half-life of 6 hours. If the remaining undecayed mass after 24 hours is 5 g, what was the initial mass of the tracer?
questions.explanation: A duration of 24 hours corresponds to 4 half-lives (24 divided by 6). Working backward, double the final mass 4 times: 5 to 10, then 20, then 40, and finally 80 g.

questions.question: If a radioactive substance has a very short half-life of 2 seconds, what does this indicate about its behavior compared to an isotope with a long half-life?
options: It decays at a much slower rate
It decays at a much faster rate
It changes its protons every second
questions.explanation: A shorter half-life means that the unstable nuclei decay much more rapidly over time, resulting in a highly intense but short-lived burst of activity.

questions.question: A sample of a radioactive element takes 24 days for its activity to fall to one-eighth of its starting value. What is the half-life of this element?
questions.explanation: A reduction to one-eighth represents exactly 3 half-lives. If 3 half-lives take 24 days, then the duration of a single half-life is 24 divided by 3, which equals 8 days.

questions.question: Which of the following natural background radiation components originates directly from cosmic rays?
options: Radiation from underground clay piping lines
Radon gas leaking from concrete paths
Chemical isotopes within specialized medical kits
High-energy radiation originating from the Sun
questions.explanation: Cosmic rays are a form of natural background radiation consisting of high-energy particles entering Earth's atmosphere from outer space and the Sun.

questions.question: The background count rate is 25 counts per minute. A total rate of 125 counts per minute is recorded near a sample. What is the corrected count rate?
questions.explanation: The true activity of the source is isolated by removing the environmental background: 125 total counts minus 25 background counts equals 100 counts per minute.

questions.question: A material has a half-life of 5 days. If a laboratory stores 64 g of this material, what mass will have DECAYED away after a period of 15 days?
questions.explanation: A period of 15 days equals 3 half-lives. The remaining mass equals 64 divided by 8, which is 8 g. Therefore, the mass that has decayed away equals 64 minus 8, which is 56 g.

questions.question: A counter records a total of 180 counts per minute near a source. If the true corrected activity of the source is 155 counts per minute, find the background rate.
questions.explanation: Since Total Count equals Source Count plus Background, the background rate is found by subtraction: 180 total minus 155 source equals 25 counts per minute.

questions.question: If a radioactive isotope has an extremely long half-life of several billion years, what can be deduced about its stability?
options: It converts into a gas within seconds
It presents an instant explosion hazard
It decays fully within one single week
It decays very slowly over generations
questions.explanation: An extremely long half-life means that the isotope is relatively stable and its nuclei decay at an incredibly slow rate, posing a long-term low-level radiation profile.
